title: Could Any Ocean Giant Actually Swallow You? (The Shoulder Test)

scenes.notes: Hook wide | starts on VO line H1 | You're about to be fed to six ocean giants. There's one test your shoulders have to pass: will they fit down the throat?

Rules card | starts on VO line R2 | The rules: just you, nothing in your hands or pockets, no gear.

scenes.notes: Gauge reveal | starts on VO line R3 | Across the muscle, your shoulders are about forty-five centimetres: a party-size pizza box.
Smaller adult | starts on VO line R4 | Smaller adults are closer to forty. Hold on to that.
Gauge rule + empty board | starts on VO line R5 | To pass, a throat must open wider than this red ring, and every giant gets the most generous estimate we could find.
Size | starts on VO line B1 | Number six: the biggest animal known to have ever lived. The blue whale.
Scale compare | starts on VO line B2 | Around thirty metres. That's two and a half school buses, nose to tail.
Lunge | starts on VO line B3 | One lunge can take in more water than the whale itself weighs, and you'd be one small part of it.
2P scenario | starts on VO line B4 | So you're floating at the surface. A shadow rises under you, the jaw drops, and you go in with the water.
Micro-loop | starts on VO line B5 | So what stops you? The throat.

scenes.notes: Gauge #6 | starts on VO line B7 | Most estimates put it somewhere between a grapefruit and a dinner plate. The widest claim out there is a small beach ball, about thirty-five centimetres. We'll take it. Your shoulders still win by more than a hand's width.

Baleen flush | starts on VO line B10 | The whale pushes the water out through its baleen and keeps the krill, and you are a very large, very confusing krill. Out you go with the seawater. Wet, alive and deeply offended.
Appetite | starts on VO line B12 | And it won't miss you. In feeding season it eats about sixteen tonnes of krill a day, ten cars' worth.
Verdict #6 | starts on VO line B13 | Biggest animal ever, and it tops out at thirty-five. Size isn't your problem.

scenes.notes: Withheld noun + bomb carbon | starts on VO line W1 | Number five comes with a strange birth certificate. For decades nobody could tell how old these fish get. Then, in 2020, researchers dated the rings in their spines using carbon that Cold War bomb tests left in the sea. One of them had been alive for about fifty years.
Size | starts on VO line W5 | Meet the whale shark. No fish alive is bigger: it grows to about eighteen metres, with a mouth a metre and a half wide, almost your height.

scenes.notes: Gauge #5 from inside | starts on VO line W7 | From inside, the view is a sieve: spongy filter pads in front of the gills, and somewhere behind them, the throat. Estimates for it run from a quarter to a cereal bowl, fifteen centimetres at the very most. A cereal bowl against a pizza box. That's not a contest, it's a misunderstanding.
Exit | starts on VO line W10 | The water leaves through the gills, and you leave the way you came in.
Verdict #5 (drop) | starts on VO line W11 | Fifteen centimetres, nowhere near you. It drops in under the blue whale.

The second-biggest fish in the sea cruises for hours with its mouth open a metre wide, wide enough for you to swim into. It strains about two million litres of water an hour, most of an Olympic pool.

scenes.notes: Speed bump | starts on VO line K4 | So why don't you end up inside? It doesn't gulp or suck. It swims with the door open, and the door is a comb of gill rakers. Drift in and you're not food. You're a speed bump.

scenes.notes: Sea monster (gross-out) | starts on VO line K8 | Here's how little sits behind that face. In 1977 a Japanese trawler hauled up a rotting carcass off New Zealand: long neck, four flippers. The papers called it a sea monster.

scenes.notes: Rot diagram + gauge | starts on VO line K9 | Tissue tests said basking shark. As one rots, the jaws and gills drop away first, leaving something that looks like a dinosaur. Take away that mouth and there isn't much throat. One old museum account puts it at about ten centimetres, with a sharp bend.
Verdict #4 (sawtooth drop) | starts on VO line K11 | The scariest mouth on the list, and it ends up at the very bottom, below even the whale shark.

scenes.notes: Re-immersion (escalates) | starts on VO line X1 | Now picture the opening again: just you, and six shadows. Three have already passed over you. The three still circling are different. The next one has had people in its mouth. The one after that inhales. And the last one has teeth.

scenes.notes: Gauge first (#3) | starts on VO line U1 | Number three. The humpback. Run the gauge first. A humpback's throat is normally about the size of your fist. Stretched for a big meal, the widest figure published is about thirty-eight centimetres. The widest throat yet, and still most of a hand short. Even a smaller adult, at forty, doesn't go down.

Real cases (composite) | starts on VO line U5 | Which is why both people known to have been inside one lived to tell you about it. A diver hunting lobster off Cape Cod in 2021, and a kayaker in the Strait of Magellan in 2025. Each was back in open water within a minute.

scenes.notes: Lunge + word gag | starts on VO line U7 | Humpbacks lunge through schools of fish with their mouths wide open, and now and then, you're one of the fish. Biologists call that engulfed, not swallowed. It's the whale version of biting a sandwich and finding a sock.
Verdict #3 (record) | starts on VO line U10 | Thirty-eight centimetres, the record so far. A lifeguard with a very large mouth.

scenes.notes: Size (#2) | starts on VO line G1 | Number two is smaller than anything yet. The goliath grouper. Up to about two and a half metres and around three hundred and sixty kilos. A grand piano with fins.

scenes.notes: Suction | starts on VO line G3 | Every giant so far was a strainer. This is the first one that inhales, and you're right in front of it. It flares its mouth so fast that the water rushes in, and so does whatever is in front of it: lobsters, fish, turtles, sharks.
Proof | starts on VO line G5 | Off southwest Florida, an angler filmed one take a hooked blacktip shark more than a metre long in a single gulp.
2P wreck | starts on VO line G6 | So you're drifting over a wreck. Something the size of a sofa slides out from under the hull.

Micro-loop + gauge #2 | starts on VO line G8 | So how wide does that mouth open? Nobody knows. No one has published a gape for a giant one. Scale up a smaller grouper and you get about forty centimetres, and that's a guess. Forty. Remember the number you were holding on to? At forty-five, you go in head first until your shoulders hit the corners of the jaw, and everything stops. At forty, on paper, it's too close to call.

scenes.notes: Folklore + ban | starts on VO line G13 | Dive boats are full of stories about groupers swallowing people like you. We couldn't find a single one that holds up. Their real problem is us. They were fished so hard that the United States banned harvesting them in 1990.
Verdict #2 (asterisk) | starts on VO line G15 | Forty, give or take a lot. It edges past the humpback, with an asterisk.
Size (#1) | starts on VO line S1 | Number one. The one you've been waiting for. The sperm whale. Up to about sixteen metres and forty tonnes, three school buses' worth.

layers.markup: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 260" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><ellipse cx="200" cy="130" rx="190" ry="120" fill="#2a1a20" stroke="#6b3a44" stroke-width="6"/></svg>

scenes.notes: Prey | starts on VO line S3 | And unlike everything so far, it hunts things bigger than you. Giant squid. In 1955, whalers off the Azores found a giant squid inside one, nearly whole, about ten metres long with its tentacles. Its weight was reported at around a hundred and eighty kilos. More than two of you.

Gauge #1: no number | starts on VO line S6 | So, what does the ring say? Nothing. Nobody has measured it. The closest we have is the anatomist Joy Reidenberg, who says a very big adult bull could swallow a person. But she means one of eighteen metres or more, bigger than most bulls anyone sees.
Honest hedge | starts on VO line S10 | And here's the honest part: nobody has ever watched one feed, so even 'it swallows prey whole' is an educated guess.

props.text: THE ONE THROAT THE GAUGE CAN'T MEASURE

scenes.notes: Ring retired | starts on VO line S11 | So you put the ring down. This is the one throat the gauge can't measure.
Verdict #1 | starts on VO line S12 | Could the biggest bulls fit you? Possibly. Has one ever? Two centuries of whaling records hold no reliable case. Top of the board, with a question mark.
Reassurance flip | starts on VO line F1 | And it wouldn't even be trying. You're not on its menu. You're barely in its way.

Twist (tone drop) | starts on VO line V1 | That should be the end, and you should be swimming home. But the board still has one empty space, above the line. So has a sperm whale ever swallowed something heavier than you? Yes.

scenes.notes: Villain swap | starts on VO line V9 | Nothing in the ocean is swallowing people whole. But it is swallowing what people leave behind, one flip-flop at a time.

Final board | starts on VO line E1 | So, the final board. Basking shark, ten centimetres. Whale shark, a cereal bowl. Blue whale, a beach ball at best. Humpback, the record. Grouper, the record with an asterisk. Sperm whale, a question mark. And above the line, our rubbish.
Bookend | starts on VO line E3 | Six giants, one pizza box of shoulders, and you get to swim home.
CTA | starts on VO line C1 | Which giant should we hold the ring up to next? Tell us in the comments. Just don't say the blue whale. It's still looking for that very confusing krill.
